## Personality

Practical, thrifty and unshakeable. She knows how many arrows the Guard has to the last fletching.

## Lore

Helewise is forty-nine, Quartermaster of the Royal Guard, and she knows how many arrows the Guard has to the last fletching. She also knows how many boots, helms, blankets, horseshoes, spoons and sacks of oats it has, and which of them are wearing thin, and who signed for the last whetstone and has not brought it back. She feeds, arms and clothes the whole Guard from a long storeroom under the Knights' Court, behind a counter with a ledger chained to it, and nothing leaves that room without her knowing. She is practical, thrifty and unshakeable, and the only person in the Court whom even Captain Rhys knocks before disturbing.

### Counted from a cradle

She grew up in the Crown Market, behind a dry-goods stall where her mother sold beans, lentils and dried peas by the scoop. Her mother, dead these many years now, had her counting scoops before she could read and haggling with carters before she could reach the counter, and Helewise has never lost the habit of believing that every coin is worth arguing for. She came to the Knights' Court at twenty as a clerk to the stores, because the Guard needed someone who could count, and she rose through the storeroom the way other guards rise through the ranks. She has been Quartermaster for fourteen years.

She haggles with the Crown Market's armourers as if the gold were her own. Her chief victim, and favourite opponent, is Vessa the armourer, who fits mail, helms and boots while her customers wait and who runs one of the two busiest forges in the market. The other belongs to Vessa's sister Selene, the weaponsmith, and the two sisters compete over everything. Helewise knows it and uses it shamelessly. She buys the Guard's mail from Vessa while mentioning, once, lightly, what Selene charges for blades; she buys the blades from Selene while wondering aloud what Vessa would say. Vessa calls her a bandit. Helewise calls it housekeeping.

### Bertrand

Her husband is Bertrand, the Drill Sergeant, who bellows at recruits at dawn and swears he can make a guard of anyone given a year and enough porridge. They met nineteen years ago over that porridge. He was demanding more for his recruits; she explained to him, to the last spoonful, exactly how much there was. She won. She usually does. They married that same year, and they have no children, and both of them say, separately and in the same tone, that a few hundred recruits through the yard is plenty.

She knows him better than anyone. She knows not to speak to him on the evenings when the patrol reports come in and he checks the names against his list, and she knows what it means when he goes quiet and marks a margin. On those evenings she makes his supper without asking and sits with him without talking, and the next morning she quietly sends a new pair of boots to the recruit he will shout at hardest.

### The boots

Lately the numbers will not come right. Patrols ride further and fight more, and they are wearing out boots faster than Helewise can buy them, along with saddle leather, shield straps and cloaks torn by things that are not branches. The Guard has more recruits than it has ever had, and every one of them needs fitting. She has stretched the budget, patched what can be patched and haggled Vessa down until even Vessa looked tired. It is still not enough, and Helewise, who has never in her life let a column of figures beat her, is beginning to suspect that this one might.

### What she wants and fears

Helewise wants every guard who rides out of the Court to ride out properly shod, properly fed and properly armed, and to come back the same way. What she fears is the day she has to tell Rhys that the Guard cannot equip the next intake, and see in his face that he already knows.

A quest might begin with Helewise needing a cartload of leather brought in from outside the city, because the market has run short, or with a crate of arrows that her ledger says was delivered and her storeroom says was not.
